extracted.intended_audience: judges, jurors, and patent litigators (trial practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and glossarial definitions for determining patent validity (e.g., obviousness, inventorship), and for calculating patent damages (lost profits, reasonable royalties, price erosion, commencement, and indirect infringement damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field [at the time the application was filed] [as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention] [as of (insert date)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court makes the ultimate legal determination of obviousness based on factual findings. The jury (if asked) should be presented with the underlying factual issues as specifically as possible. For post-AIA claims use the effective filing date option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the level of ordinary skill that someone would have had [at the time the claimed invention was made] [as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all evidence introduced at trial, including (1) levels of education and experience of persons working in the field; (2) types of problems encountered in the field; and (3) sophistication of the technology. Parties may present differing contentions about the level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which references are within the scope and content of the prior art to be used in evaluating validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References must be reasonably related to the claimed invention (i.e., in the same field or from another field to which a person of ordinary skill would look to solve a known problem). Present only the Graham factors that are actually in dispute to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what difference, if any, existed between the claimed invention and the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If dispute is limited to a specific claim limitation, present only that issue as the 'difference' factor. Consider whether a prior art reference discloses particular claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) bearing on obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider evidence of objective indicia that may bear on nonobviousness or obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of possible factors: (1) commercial success due to merits of the claimed invention; (2) long-felt need for the solution; (3) unsuccessful attempts by others; (4) copying by others; (5) unexpected and superior results; (6) acceptance by others as shown by praise or licensing; (7) other evidence tending to show nonobviousness; (8) independent invention by others before or about the same time; (9) other evidence tending to show obviousness. Presence of factors 1–7 may indicate nonobviousness; presence of 8–9 may indicate obviousness. Relevance and weight are for the factfinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining known elements (reason to combine / motivation to combine)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim composed of several elements is not proved obvious merely by showing each element was independently known in the prior art; consider whether there was a reason for a person of ordinary skill to combine elements as in the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether there is teaching, suggestion, or motivation in prior art to make the claimed modification or combination, whether the change was predictable use of prior art elements, whether a known technique was applied as before, and whether the claimed invention would have been 'obvious to try' with a reasonable expectation of success. Be careful to avoid hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time reference for obviousness determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether obviousness is judged as of the time the claimed invention was made or as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the effective filing date option for post-AIA claims (effective filing dates on or after March 16, 2013). Put yourself in the position of a person of ordinary skill at that time and do not consider later knowledge or the patent's teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be invalid if it fails to name all actual inventors and only the actual inventors; to be an inventor, one must make a significant contribution to the conception of one or more claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons may be inventors even if they did not work together or make the same type/amount of contribution. Mere assistance in experimentation, following instructions, or explaining well-known concepts does not make one an inventor. For corrective or state-law claims, the plaintiff must show it is highly probable they are an actual inventor. Corroborating evidence of a contemporaneous disclosure enabling one skilled in the art is required and judged under a rule of reason analysis. Correction of inventorship is generally a matter for the court, not the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages measure — compensatory principle and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must adequately compensate the patent holder for the infringement and should put the patent holder in approximately the financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred; damages may not be less than a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent holder bears the burden to persuade the factfinder of the amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence. Damages must be proven with reasonable certainty (not mathematical precision) and may not be remote or speculative. Damages are compensatory, not punitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — general but-for test
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits, the patent holder must show that but for the infringement there is a reasonable probability it would have made the sales that the infringer made of the infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder must establish the share of the infringer's sales it would have made if the infringing product were not on the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — factors to prove lost profits (Panduit-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holder is entitled to lost profits if it proves: (1) demand for the patented product/method; (2) no acceptable non-infringing substitutes (or the amount it would have made despite substitutes); (3) the patent holder had the manufacturing and marketing capacity to make the infringing sales; (4) the amount of profit the patent holder would have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable non-infringing substitute may be available even if not on sale during infringement if material, experience, and know-how were readily available and customers would have believed it acceptable. Consider factors that suggest availability (or unavailability), including cost, customer acceptance, and whether the alleged infringer had to design or invent around the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — market share proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to prove the number of sales the patent holder would have made is to prove its market share (excluding infringing products) and award a share of profits equal to that market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which products are in the relevant market. Products are in the same market if they are sufficiently similar to compete against each other — i.e., neither has a significantly higher price nor substantially different characteristics than the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — collateral products
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits for collateral products (products the patent holder would have sold along with the patented product), the patent holder must prove (1) it is more likely than not that it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral product and the patented product together must be analogous to components of a single assembly, parts of a complete machine, or constitute a functional unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral-sales recovery requires linking the collateral product to the patented product as part of a functional or assembled unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — price erosion damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holder can recover additional damages if it shows with reasonable probability that, absent the infringement, it would have charged higher prices for some products; damages may include the profit differential and any increased costs caused by competition (e.g., additional marketing costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When calculating total losses from price erosion, account for any drop in sales that would have resulted from a higher price. If price erosion is found, the higher price may also be used in determining lost profits from sales lost due to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — entitlement when lost profits absent or partial
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent holder has not proved lost profits (or only proved them for part of the infringing sales), the patent holder is entitled to a reasonable royalty for the infringing sales not covered by lost profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable royalty is a separate entitlement and fills the gap where lost profits are not established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — definition and hypothetical negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the payment for a license that would have resulted from a hypothetical negotiation between the patent holder and the infringer at the time the infringing activity first began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume both parties acted reasonably and believed the patent was valid and infringed. The test is what the negotiation would have produced, not what either party preferred. Royalties may be computed as ongoing percentage-based royalties or fixed lump-sum payments. The factfinder chooses the method most appropriate based on evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — base and rate considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute an ongoing royalty determine the 'base' (the product revenue subject to the royalty) and the 'rate' (percentage or per-unit amount) that would have resulted from the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent covers only a component or feature of a product, the base would normally be that component's revenue. However, if the patented feature is the reason customers buy the whole product or the feature's value cannot be separated, the base could be whole-product revenue (with a correspondingly lower rate). Examples: per-unit calculations, percentage of revenue, or lump-sum for past and future sales. Choose the approach best supported by the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of commencement for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages commence on the date the alleged infringer both infringed and was notified of the patent (various marking/notice scenarios apply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the commencement date based on whether the patent holder sold a product marked with the patent number, provided actual written notice, or the patent was granted before or after the infringing activity began. Different rules may apply for method claims or for indirect infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for inducement or contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover damages for induced infringement, the patent holder must prove the accused product necessarily infringes the patent or prove acts of direct infringement by others induced by the accused infringer; liabilities are limited by the number of instances of direct infringement. Similarly, for contributory infringement the patent holder must prove the accused product necessarily infringes or that the accused made a substantial contribution to others' direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because damages for these forms of infringement are limited by the number of direct acts, the patent holder must further prove the number of direct acts of infringement (e.g., by showing individual acts or demonstrating that a class of products/uses directly infringes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — glossary definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation exists when a claimed invention describes an earlier invention and therefore is not new and is not entitled to be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is a distinct ground of invalidity (novelty) from obviousness and requires that a single prior art reference disclose every claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant had a best mode for practicing the invention as of the time the application was first filed, that best mode must be set forth in the patent specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode refers to the best way the inventor actually knew to make or use the invention at the time of filing; failure to disclose an existing best mode can be a basis for invalidity or correction depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification of the patent must contain a description sufficient to enable persons skilled in the field of the invention to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement ensures the patent disclosure is adequate to teach the invention to one skilled in the art; lack of enablement is a ground of invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim / Elements — infringement test
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim is a concise formal definition of an invention; a device or method infringes a patent if it contains each and every required part (element) or step of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may be independent or dependent. A dependent claim incorporates the limitations of the referenced claim(s). For infringement, all claim limitations must be present in the accused device or method.
